title: Build a Home Cafe
description: Furnish an imaginary corner cafe through six scenarios and two rankings, then see where your choices fall on two scales: Familiar to Experimental, and Private Retreat to Shared Hangout.

sections.title: Furnish the cafe
sections.description: Layout, menu and atmosphere

sections.title: Set your priorities
sections.description: What matters most to you as a host

dimensions.description: Whether you lean toward dependable favorites and settled routines, or toward changing menus, odd finds and new recipes.
Whether your cafe is mostly a quiet personal refuge, or a lively place built around company and conversation.

questions.prompt: Your tiny cafe has one free wall. What goes on it?
questions.explanation: A wall sets the tone. Each option leans settled or adventurous, and private or social, by how it invites people to use the room.

options.label: A chalkboard of well-loved house drinks that regulars order by name
A shelf of mismatched thrifted mugs you rotate for your own cup
A record player where guests take turns picking
A cozy reading nook with a small "quiet corner" sign

questions.prompt: Now arrange the seating. Which layout would you build first?
questions.explanation: Seating shapes who talks to whom. Your choice shows whether you design for solitude, for company, or for watching something interesting happen.

options.label: One deep armchair by the window with a side table
A long shared table where everyone sits together
Counter stools facing the brewing station to watch experiments
Two small curtained nooks for private chats

questions.prompt: Plan the menu. Which approach feels most like your cafe?
questions.explanation: A menu philosophy reveals how much you value repetition and mastery versus novelty, and whether drinks are meant to be shared or savored alone.

options.label: Three dependable drinks, each made the same careful way
A new experimental drink every single week
Tasting flights that tables split and compare
One signature cup, made just for quiet mornings

questions.prompt: Match each atmosphere detail to the feeling you want it to create.
questions.explanation: Pairing details with feelings shows where you want predictability or surprise, and whether the room invites conversation or calm.

questions.prompt: On a typical afternoon, how full should your cafe feel?
questions.explanation: There is no right crowd size. This slider simply records how much company you picture around your cups.

questions.prompt: A guest asks for a drink that is not on your menu. What do you do?
questions.explanation: Handling an off-menu request shows whether you reach for a trusted standard, improvise something new, and whether you do it quietly or together.

options.label: Bring your standard cup quietly to their table
Invite them behind the counter to invent something together
Try a new twist on your own and serve it with a note
Suggest a familiar favorite and chat while it brews

questions.prompt: Rank these cafe features from most to least important to you.
questions.explanation: Your ordering shows which parts of the cafe you would protect first: personal comfort, private tinkering, regular gatherings or lively events.

items.label: A comfy corner only you use
A notebook for testing new recipes alone
A monthly open tasting night with new drinks

questions.prompt: You can improve one thing next. Rank these from first priority to last.
questions.explanation: This ordering shows where you would put effort next: refining a favorite, hunting for novelty, making room for friends or protecting quiet time.

items.label: Setting aside quiet hours with the door closed

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: This is a preference game with no right or wrong answers. The cafe scenarios are invented, and the two scales only summarize your own choices in this session.

title: Kitchen Tool Detective
description: Read the evidence left on a board, bowl or plate and name the tool that could have produced it, then judge when the evidence alone cannot prove the tool.

sections.title: Case files
sections.description: Six cases where the evidence points to one tool.

sections.title: Evidence checks
sections.description: Two cases about what the evidence can and cannot prove.

questions.prompt: Which listed tool is designed to produce adjustable thin slices?
questions.context: Case 1: a plate holds cucumber rounds, each paper-thin and identical. Tool cards: mandoline (flat blade over a plate whose height you set), whisk (looped wires), ladle (deep bowl on a long handle), rolling pin (smooth cylinder).
questions.explanation: A mandoline's blade sits over an adjustable-height surface, so the same thin thickness repeats slice after slice. The other tools mix, scoop or flatten instead of slicing.

questions.prompt: Which tool most plausibly left this evidence?
questions.context: Case 2: flour was dusted evenly over a counter. A few small, hard lumps were left behind inside a round tool with a fine wire mesh. The lumps were too large to pass through.
questions.explanation: A sieve passes fine particles through its mesh and holds back lumps. A rolling pin, ladle or zester would not separate lumps from flour this way.

questions.prompt: A pile of tiny, fragrant strands of lemon peel sits on a plate, with white pith untouched. Which tool made them?
questions.context: Case 3: the lemon itself is still nearly whole, with only the outer coloured layer scraped away in fine threads.
questions.explanation: A zester has small sharp holes that shave only the thin coloured outer layer into fine strands. A masher, ladle or tongs cannot remove peel in threads.

questions.prompt: Which tool fits the evidence: pasta nests lifted from a pot, each with two opposite pinch dents?
questions.context: Case 4: the nests are intact and dry-surfaced, with no broken strands. Each shows two small dents on opposite sides, as if gripped between two arms. The pot water was not scooped out.
questions.explanation: Tongs squeeze from two sides, leaving paired opposite dents while lifting a whole item. A ladle would scoop liquid, and a pin or whisk would not grip.

questions.prompt: Match each piece of evidence to the tool that could produce it.
questions.context: Case 5: four results were found on one counter. Several may come from the same tool. Tools: mandoline (adjustable-gap slicer), ladle (scoops liquid), rolling pin (flattens dough).
questions.explanation: Dial-set thin ribbons and identical rounds both point to the mandoline. Moving soup without tipping the pot is a ladle job. An even flat dough sheet suggests a rolling pin.

left.label: Soup moved to bowls without tipping the pot
Cookie dough pressed into an even flat sheet
Cabbage ribbons, thickness set by a dial gap

questions.prompt: For each piece of evidence, choose the tool that fits.
questions.context: Case 6: three separate results. Assume the measuring jug is marked in millilitres, as declared metric kitchen units. Do not assume a millilitre mark means the same weight for every food.
questions.explanation: Mashing leaves chunky pieces, a marked jug portions liquid volume in declared units, and a peeler removes a wide thin ribbon of peel.

cells.label: Mashed potato with a few intact chunks
Exactly 250 mL of milk read off printed lines
A wide, thin ribbon of apple skin

questions.prompt: Which conclusion does the evidence support?
questions.context: Case 7: a bowl holds a smooth, creamy dressing in which tiny oil droplets are spread through vinegar, with an emulsifier added. Possible mixers in the kitchen: a whisk, a sealed jar for shaking, and a blender.
questions.explanation: The droplets show an emulsion, which an emulsifier can help keep from merging. Whisking, shaking or blending could each disperse the droplets, so the result alone cannot name the tool.

options.label: It is an emulsion, but whisk, jar or blender could each have made it
A ladle must have stirred it

questions.prompt: Connect each clue to every tool that could still explain it.
questions.context: Case 8: tool cards. Knife: cuts on a board, any shape. Food-processor disc: cuts cubes or slices inside a bowl. Mandoline: makes slices only, on its own plate. Only the knife blade touches a board.
questions.explanation: Cubes rule out the mandoline, which only slices. Flat slices fit all three tools. Score marks on a board fit only the knife, since the other two cut elsewhere.

left.label: Score marks on the board beneath the pile

Exploratorium: emulsions

note: All cases are invented scenarios, with the tool cards supplied in each task. Your result is your score out of 8, and each task explains the tool reasoning.

title: Flavor Triangle
description: Match taste terms, rescue off-balance fictional dishes, and test two kitchen ideas, then choose your own flavor direction in four taste tradeoffs.

sections.title: Rescue the dish
sections.description: Four knowledge tasks with correct answers.

sections.title: Your taste direction
sections.description: Four preference tasks with no right answers.

dimensions.description: Whether you tend to finish dishes with rich, mellow, sweet notes or with a sour, zesty lift.
Whether you prefer gentle, quiet seasoning or loud, assertive flavors.

questions.prompt: Match each basic taste term to the everyday description that fits it.
questions.explanation: Sour is the acidic tang of foods like lemon, salty is the taste of salt, sweet is sugary, and bitter is the sharp edge of dark coffee.

right.label: The tang of lemon juice or vinegar
The taste of sugar or honey
The sharp edge of black coffee

questions.prompt: Using the tasting card, match each fictional dish problem to the adjustment the card recommends.
questions.context: Invented tasting card: heavy or greasy dishes need acid. Puckering sour dishes need a little sweetener or fat. Dull dishes with clearly too little salt need salt.
questions.explanation: The card pairs heavy and greasy dishes with acid, puckery dishes with sweetener or fat, and under-salted dishes with salt. Two dishes can share the same fix.

right.label: Add a little sweetener or fat

questions.prompt: Compared with the start, how salty is each cup of the reduced stock?
questions.context: Invented recipe: 4 cups of stock get 1 teaspoon of salt, then simmer uncovered until 2 cups remain. Assume only water leaves as steam and all the salt stays.
questions.explanation: The same amount of salt is now in half the liquid, so each cup holds twice as much salt. Cooking can change a dish's composition this way.

options.label: Four times as salty per cup

questions.prompt: In this dressing, what does the mustard emulsifier do?
questions.context: Invented recipe card: oil is shaken into lemon juice until tiny oil droplets spread through the juice. A spoonful of mustard is added as the emulsifier.
questions.explanation: An emulsion has droplets of one liquid dispersed in another, and an emulsifier can inhibit those droplets from merging back together.

options.label: It helps keep the droplets from merging back together
It turns the oil into water
It removes all sourness from the juice

questions.prompt: Your fictional tomato soup tastes balanced. Which finishing touch would you reach for?
questions.explanation: No answer is right here. Lemon leans bright, cream leans round, chili flakes lean bold, and plain herbs lean subtle.

questions.prompt: Your fictional soup is balanced. Would you nudge it toward sweet roundness or tangy brightness?
questions.explanation: This is a pure taste preference. Slide toward roundness for mellow, sweet notes or toward brightness for a tangy, zesty lift.

questions.prompt: Rank these fictional dishes from the one you would most like to eat to the one you would least like.
questions.explanation: There is no correct order. Each dish mixes a bright or round character with a subtle or bold one, so your ranking shows your direction.

items.label: Tamarind-lime noodle salad with sharp chilies
Creamy corn chowder with gentle seasoning
Smoky peanut-chili stew with brown sugar
Cucumber slices in light rice vinegar

questions.prompt: When you season your own fictional dish, do you stay quiet and gentle or go loud?
questions.explanation: Neither end is better. Subtle seasoning lets main ingredients speak softly, while bold seasoning makes flavors assertive and memorable.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data
Exploratorium: cooking science
Exploratorium: emulsions

note: The first four tasks are scored for accuracy. The last four are taste preferences with no correct answers, and they are shown separately as your Bright vs Round and Subtle vs Bold direction. Recipes and tasting cards are invented, and the advice reflects common practice, not strict rules.

title: Fridge-to-Meal Puzzle
description: Solve clue-driven puzzles that turn a fictional fridge into dinners without repeating or wasting a thing. Fill grids, repair broken clue sets, and deduce what must be true.

sections.title: Fill the Fridge
sections.description: Allocate each card to a dinner using the clues.

sections.title: Repair the Puzzle
sections.description: Find the change that fixes a broken clue set.

sections.title: Final Dinners
sections.description: Harder allocations and what-must-be-true deductions.

questions.prompt: Assign each fridge card to Dinner A or Dinner B so every card is used once.
questions.context: Invented puzzle. Cards: eggs, rice, scallions, cheese. Each dinner gets exactly two cards. Clue 1: Dinner A has no cheese. Clue 2: Dinner B uses rice.
questions.explanation: Cheese cannot go in A, and rice is in B, so B is rice plus cheese. That leaves eggs and scallions for A.

questions.prompt: Give each key card to exactly one dinner, using all five clues.
questions.context: Invented puzzle. Cards: noodles, cabbage, tomatoes, tortillas. Dinners: Soup, Wrap, Salad, Stir-fry, one card each. Soup gets neither tomatoes nor tortillas. Noodles are not in Salad or Wrap. Cabbage is not in Soup. Tortillas are not in Salad or Stir-fry. Tomatoes are not in Stir-fry.
questions.explanation: Soup can only take noodles or cabbage, and cabbage is barred, so Soup is noodles. Tortillas must go to Wrap, and the tomato clue sends cabbage to Stir-fry.

questions.prompt: Split six cards across three dinners, two per dinner, so every clue holds.
questions.context: Invented puzzle. Cards: carrots, quinoa, yogurt, mint, chickpeas, lemon. Dinners: Bowl, Dip, Salad, two cards each. Yogurt and mint share a dinner. Chickpeas are not in Salad. Carrots and lemon are in different dinners. Quinoa is in Bowl. Lemon is not in Bowl.
questions.explanation: Bowl needs one more card besides quinoa; it cannot be lemon, yogurt or mint, and chickpeas would force carrots with lemon. So carrots join quinoa; chickpeas and lemon take Dip, leaving Salad for yogurt and mint.

questions.prompt: No assignment fits these clues. Keeping clues 1–3 unchanged, which new clue 4 gives exactly one solution?
questions.context: Invented puzzle. Cards: eggs, rice, cheese; dinners: Omelet, Fried Rice, Quesadilla, one card each. Clue 1: Quesadilla gets neither eggs nor rice. Clue 2: Omelet does not get cheese. Clue 3: Omelet does not get eggs. Clue 4: Fried Rice does not get eggs.
questions.explanation: Clues 1–3 force Quesadilla to cheese and Omelet to rice, which leaves eggs for Fried Rice. Only barring cheese from Fried Rice allows that.

options.label: Fried Rice does not get cheese
Fried Rice gets neither eggs nor rice
Fried Rice does not get eggs or cheese

questions.prompt: Removing which single clue leaves exactly one valid weekly schedule?
questions.context: Invented puzzle. Beans, corn and squash fill Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, one per day. Clues: (1) Beans are on Monday. (2) Corn is on Monday. (3) Squash is not on Tuesday. (4) Corn is not on Tuesday.
questions.explanation: Clues 1 and 2 clash over Monday. Dropping clue 1 gives corn Monday, squash Wednesday, beans Tuesday. Dropping clue 2 forces corn onto Tuesday, which clue 4 forbids.

questions.prompt: Using the recipe cards and clue, match each dinner to the one extra card it receives.
questions.context: Invented recipe cards list allowed extras. Tacos: cilantro or banana. Pasta: basil or cilantro. Curry: coconut milk or cilantro. Pancakes: banana or coconut milk. Each extra is used once. Clue: Pancakes do not get banana.
questions.explanation: Basil fits only Pasta. Pancakes cannot take banana, so they take coconut milk. Banana then must go to Tacos, leaving cilantro for Curry.

questions.prompt: The clues leave two valid splits. Which extra clue leaves exactly one?
questions.context: Invented puzzle. Cards: peppers, onions, corn, tofu. Dinner A and Dinner B each get two cards. Tofu is not in A. Peppers and onions are not in the same dinner.
questions.explanation: A must be corn plus peppers or corn plus onions. Putting onions in B leaves only peppers and corn in A. The other options give zero solutions or leave both splits.

options.label: Peppers and onions are in Dinner A

questions.prompt: Which statement must be true in every valid schedule?
questions.context: Invented puzzle. Rice, noodles, potatoes and bread fill Monday to Thursday, one per day. Noodles come earlier than rice. Rice comes earlier than bread. Potatoes are not on Monday or Thursday.
questions.explanation: Potatoes take Tuesday or Wednesday, and noodles, rice, bread keep that order in the other three days. Either way noodles are first on Monday; the other statements change between schedules.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All fridges, recipe cards and dinners here are invented puzzle pieces. They make no diet, safety, storage or cooking claims.

title: Grocery Aisle Time Machine
description: Use dated clues from an invented grocery chain to order store changes, match features to the problems they solved, and name the era of checkout scenes.

questions.prompt: Order these changes at the invented Brindle Market chain from earliest to latest.
questions.context: Clues: Self-serve shelves opened first. Cart corrals were added after self-serve shelves but before scan-code checkout. Scan-code checkout began 9 years before phone pickup lanes.
questions.explanation: Self-serve shelves come first, corrals sit between shelves and scanning, and scan-code checkout precedes pickup lanes by 9 years.

questions.prompt: Using the invented Harrow Foods timeline, order these four changes from earliest to latest.
questions.context: Year 0 is opening. Loyalty cards launched in Year 14. The paper-bag stand launched 6 years before loyalty cards. Self-checkout launched in twice the loyalty-card year. Delivery lockers launched 5 years after self-checkout.
questions.explanation: Bag stand is Year 8, loyalty cards Year 14, self-checkout Year 28 (2 × 14), and lockers Year 33.

questions.prompt: Match each invented store feature to the problem it was designed to address.
questions.context: In the invented Veldmark Co-op, a feature solves the problem its description directly targets. More than one feature can address the same problem.
questions.explanation: Hanging signs help shoppers find items; pre-weighed bags and code-reading checkout both cut counter waits; wheeled carts ease carrying.

left.label: Hanging signs listing each aisle's goods
Produce weighed and bagged before opening
Checkout reads a printed code instead of keying prices
Wheeled frames that hold items while shoppers walk

questions.prompt: Match each shopper problem to the invented Veldmark service that targets it.
questions.context: Services: a phone list saves editable lists; a bag-return deposit gives a coin back for returned sturdy bags; a timed pickup slot lets people collect pre-ordered goods from their car.
questions.explanation: Lists solve forgetting, deposits reduce single-use sacks, and timed car-side pickup suits both rush-hour avoidance and full-handed shoppers.

left.label: Shoppers lose track of what they meant to buy
Shoppers dislike waiting inside at rush hour
The store wants fewer new single-use sacks
A shopper with full hands wants to collect goods at the car

questions.prompt: Which era fits: a shopper hands a written list to a clerk, who fetches tins from behind the counter?
questions.context: Invented Veldmark eras, by when each feature first appeared. Counter Era: clerks fetch goods. Self-Serve Era: open shelves and carts. Scan Era: code readers and loyalty cards. Tap-and-Collect Era: phone ordering and tap payment. Pick the era of the scene's newest feature.
questions.explanation: Clerk-fetched goods are the only feature present, so nothing newer appears and the scene belongs to the Counter Era.

questions.prompt: Which era fits: a shopper pushes a cart down open aisles, and the cashier keys in every price by hand?
questions.context: Invented Veldmark eras, by when each feature first appeared. Counter Era: clerks fetch goods. Self-Serve Era: open shelves and carts. Scan Era: code readers and loyalty cards. Tap-and-Collect Era: phone ordering and tap payment. Pick the era of the scene's newest feature.
questions.explanation: Open aisles and carts began in the Self-Serve Era. Hand-keyed prices are older, and no code readers or phones appear.

questions.prompt: Which era fits: a cashier passes jars over a beeping reader while the shopper shows a loyalty card?
questions.context: Invented Veldmark eras, by when each feature first appeared. Counter Era: clerks fetch goods. Self-Serve Era: open shelves and carts. Scan Era: code readers and loyalty cards. Tap-and-Collect Era: phone ordering and tap payment. Pick the era of the scene's newest feature.
questions.explanation: Code readers and loyalty cards both debuted in the Scan Era, and nothing in the scene needs phone ordering or tap payment.

questions.prompt: Which era fits: goods ordered by phone that morning are scanned at a car-side lane, and payment is by tap?
questions.context: Invented Veldmark eras, by when each feature first appeared. Counter Era: clerks fetch goods. Self-Serve Era: open shelves and carts. Scan Era: code readers and loyalty cards. Tap-and-Collect Era: phone ordering and tap payment. Pick the era of the scene's newest feature.
questions.explanation: Scanning is older, but phone ordering and tap payment are the newest features, so the scene belongs to the Tap-and-Collect Era.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All chains, years, eras and features here are invented for the puzzles, not real shopping history. Each task gives every clue you need, so no outside knowledge is required.

title: Pantry Swap Laboratory
description: Match stand-in ingredients to the jobs a recipe needs done, choose every acceptable swap in bakes and sauces, and see your accuracy with an explanation for each task.

sections.title: Jobs and measures
sections.description: Match stand-ins to jobs, then handle an emulsion and a unit conversion.

sections.title: Bakes and sauces
sections.description: Choose every swap that covers a recipe job.

questions.prompt: A pancake recipe with baking soda has no buttermilk. Link each stand-in to every job it can cover.
questions.context: Lab cards. Milk with lemon juice: mostly water, sour, fat too small to count. Vegetable oil: pure fat, no water, not sour. Baking soda releases gas only when a sour ingredient is present.
questions.explanation: Milk with lemon juice brings liquid and sourness, so it adds tang and activates baking soda. Oil is only a fat, so it covers tenderness and nothing else.

questions.prompt: Six ingredients ran out mid-recipe. Match each stand-in to the single job it was brought in to do.
questions.context: Lab cards. Honey: sweet syrup. Mashed ripe banana: sweet fruit. Cornstarch stirred into cold water: thickens when heated. Olive oil and melted butter: fats. White vinegar: sour liquid.
questions.explanation: Honey and banana both sweeten, oil and butter both supply fat, starch in water thickens when heated, and vinegar supplies sourness. Several stand-ins can share one job.

questions.prompt: An oil and lemon juice dressing keeps separating. Which addition from the cards best keeps the droplets from merging again?
questions.context: Lab cards. Egg yolk: contains emulsifiers that coat droplets. Extra oil: more of the same liquid. Granulated sugar: dissolves in the watery part. Dried parsley flakes: dry bits with no emulsifier.
questions.explanation: An emulsion scatters droplets of one liquid in another, and an emulsifier can inhibit those droplets from merging. Of the cards, only egg yolk is an emulsifier.

questions.prompt: A buttermilk stand-in is 1 tablespoon lemon juice topped up with milk to fill 1 cup. How many millilitres of milk are needed?
questions.context: Lab unit rules: 1 tablespoon = 15 mL and 1 cup = 240 mL. Treat everything as volume only; do not convert to grams.
questions.explanation: The cup is 240 mL and the lemon juice takes up 15 mL, so the milk fills the remaining 225 mL. Adding rather than subtracting overshoots the cup.

questions.prompt: Muffin batter has run out of butter, which was giving fat, moisture and sweetness. Link each stand-in to every job it covers.
questions.context: Lab cards. Neutral oil: fat only. Unsweetened applesauce: mostly water, mildly sweet, no fat. Plain yogurt: mostly water, sour, fat too small to count.
questions.explanation: Oil is the only fat here. Applesauce brings moisture and mild sweetness, while yogurt brings moisture and tang. No single swap replaces everything butter did.

questions.prompt: A pan sauce lost its wine, which added liquid and sourness. Link each stand-in to every job it covers.
questions.context: Lab cards. Chicken stock: mostly water, not sour. Lemon juice: sour, mostly water. Cornstarch stirred into water: thickens once heated, mostly water. Cold butter: fat only. Jobs are met only if the card shows them.

right.label: Supply liquid to loosen the pan

questions.explanation: Stock, lemon juice and the starch mixture are all mostly water, so each can loosen the pan. Only lemon juice adds sourness, only starch thickens, and only butter adds fat.

questions.prompt: A cookie dough with baking soda lacks a sour ingredient, sweetener, fat and dry bulk. Link each stand-in to every job it covers.
questions.context: Lab cards. White vinegar: sour liquid. Honey: sweet syrup, neutral in sourness. Neutral oil: fat only. Ground oats: dry powder. Sweetened yogurt: sour, sweet, mostly water, fat too small to count.
questions.explanation: Baking soda needs a sour partner, which vinegar and sweetened yogurt both provide. Yogurt also sweetens, honey only sweetens, oil only adds fat, and oats only add dry bulk.

questions.prompt: A pancake batter needs a water-based liquid and a sour ingredient for its baking soda. Rate each swap.
questions.context: Lab cards. Oil: no water, not sour. Milk: mostly water, not sour. White vinegar: sour, mostly water. Citric acid powder: sour, dry, no water.
questions.explanation: Oil covers neither job, milk only supplies liquid, and the dry powder only supplies sourness. Milk plus vinegar covers both, so the baking soda can work.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

Exploratorium: emulsions
NIST: household measures

note: Ingredient cards and unit rules are simplified lab assumptions supplied in each question, not tested recipe advice. Answers depend on the cards shown, and real recipes vary.

title: The Lunchbox Across Three Borders
description: Use three invented lunch menus from Canada, Mexico and the US to link ingredients, match preparations and find what the menus share.

questions.prompt: Connect each ingredient card to every menu that includes it.
questions.context: Invented menus. Canada (Mina, Halifax): beans, cheddar, apple, carrot, rye bread. Mexico (Valeria, Monterrey): beans, tortilla, lime, carrot, avocado. US (Tessa, Tucson): beans, cheddar, apple, tortilla, corn.
questions.explanation: Cheddar is in the Canada and US menus, carrot in Canada and Mexico, tortilla in Mexico and US, and lime only in Mexico.

questions.prompt: Which ingredient card appears in all three invented menus?
questions.context: Canada: beans, cheddar, apple, carrot, rye bread. Mexico: beans, tortilla, lime, carrot, avocado. US: beans, cheddar, apple, tortilla, corn.
questions.explanation: Only beans are listed in every menu. Carrot misses the US menu, apple misses Mexico, and lime appears only in Mexico.

questions.prompt: Match each ingredient in a specific menu to how that menu prepares it.
questions.context: Canada: beans baked slowly with onion; carrot grated raw. Mexico: beans simmered then mashed; carrot simmered with rice. The same ingredient can be prepared differently in each menu.
questions.explanation: Sharing an ingredient does not mean sharing a method: both menus use beans and carrot, but each prepares them in its own way.

questions.prompt: Match each ingredient in the US menu to its preparation.
questions.context: US menu (invented): cheddar is melted inside a folded tortilla; the tortilla is crisped on a griddle; corn kernels are roasted in a dry pan; apple is sliced raw.
questions.explanation: Each US menu item has one stated preparation, so cheddar is melted, the tortilla is crisped, corn is roasted and apple stays raw.

questions.prompt: In the Mexico menu, how is the tortilla prepared?
questions.context: Mexico menu (invented): beans simmered then mashed; tortilla warmed on a dry griddle; lime squeezed over; carrot simmered with rice; avocado cubed raw.
questions.explanation: The Mexico menu only warms its tortilla. Crisping and folding around melted cheddar belong to the US menu, not this one.

questions.prompt: For each shared-ingredient card, select every menu that uses it.
questions.context: Canada: beans, cheddar, apple, carrot, rye bread. Mexico: beans, tortilla, lime, carrot, avocado. US: beans, cheddar, apple, tortilla, corn.
questions.explanation: Beans link to all three menus, apple to Canada and US, and corn only to the US menu.

questions.prompt: How many of the ingredient cards appear in exactly two of the three menus?
questions.context: Canada: beans, cheddar, apple, carrot, rye bread. Mexico: beans, tortilla, lime, carrot, avocado. US: beans, cheddar, apple, tortilla, corn.
questions.explanation: Cheddar, apple, carrot and tortilla each appear in two menus. Beans appear in three; the other cards appear in just one.

questions.prompt: Across all three invented menus, how many different ingredient cards are there in total?
questions.context: Canada: beans, cheddar, apple, carrot, rye bread. Mexico: beans, tortilla, lime, carrot, avocado. US: beans, cheddar, apple, tortilla, corn.
questions.explanation: There are 15 listings, but shared cards count once: beans, cheddar, apple, carrot, rye bread, tortilla, lime, avocado and corn make 9 different cards.

title: Texture Tournament
description: Pick between paired everyday textures, then rank texture combinations for two invented snacks to see where you land between Crisp and Soft, and between Comfort and Surprise.

dimensions.description: Whether your picks lean toward crackle, snap and crunch or toward smooth, creamy and tender textures.
Whether you favor familiar, steady textures or contrasts that burst, pop, shatter or change as you eat.

questions.prompt: Shatteringly crisp chips or silky smooth hummus? Pick one for tonight's snack.
questions.explanation: There is no right answer. Choosing crisp chips tilts your crown toward crunch; choosing hummus tilts it toward smooth, creamy textures.

questions.prompt: Which would you rather bite into on a quiet evening?
questions.explanation: Both options are soft. This pair explores familiar comfort versus an unexpected burst, rather than crispness.

options.label: Soft juice-filled pearls that gently burst

questions.prompt: Snack-bar matchup: which texture wins your vote?
questions.explanation: Crunchy clusters are a steady, familiar crunch. A stretchy, chewy bite is less predictable, so it nudges you toward surprise without moving the crisp-versus-silky axis.

questions.prompt: Dessert bracket: which spoonful gets your pick?
questions.explanation: Plain creamy yogurt is smooth and dependable. A crackly caramel shell over custard adds contrast, so it counts as crisp and surprising.

options.label: Crackly caramel shell over soft custard

questions.prompt: Lunchbox showdown: which side would you reach for first?
questions.explanation: A crisp apple slice offers a familiar, snappy crunch. A smooth pudding cup pulls toward soft, silky textures without changing how surprising your choice is.

questions.prompt: Bakery bracket: which one are you picking up?
questions.explanation: Soft bread is a cozy, familiar chew. Flaky layered pastry shatters and crumbles in surprising ways, so it leans crisp and adventurous.

questions.prompt: The invented snack "Cloud Cup" has four possible texture combos. Rank them from most to least appealing.

title: Menu Word Decoder
description: Use a short kitchen card to decode menu words like seared, braised, poached and glazed by matching terms, ordering steps, linking features and reading two menu cases.

questions.prompt: A menu line promises scallops with a deep brown crust from seconds on a blazing pan. Which word fits?
questions.context: Kitchen card: Seared = browned fast on a very hot surface. Braised = browned, then cooked slowly in a little liquid in a covered pot. Poached = fully submerged in liquid kept below a boil. Roasted = cooked by dry oven air all around.
questions.explanation: Searing means quick browning on a very hot surface. Braising and poaching rely on liquid, and roasting uses surrounding oven air rather than a hot contact surface.

questions.prompt: Match each menu word to the kitchen log line it describes.
questions.context: Kitchen card: Seared = browned fast on a very hot surface. Braised = browned, then slowly cooked in a little liquid, covered. Poached = fully submerged in liquid below a boil. Roasted = dry oven air. Glazed = coated with a shiny layer. Emulsified = droplets of one liquid dispersed in another.
questions.explanation: Each term has one defining feature on the card: browning, covered slow liquid cooking, gentle submersion, oven air, a shiny coating, or dispersed droplets.

right.label: Tuna crusted by seconds on a blazing pan
Ribs browned, then covered with a little stock for slow cooking
Pears held fully under liquid that never reaches a boil
Carrots cooked by dry air all around in an oven
Squash wedges brushed with a shiny syrup coat
Dressing with tiny oil droplets spread through vinegar

questions.prompt: Order these steps for a poached pear dessert so the menu word is honest.
questions.context: Poached means fully submerged in liquid kept below a boil. Steps are from an invented Lantern Bay Bistro recipe card.
questions.explanation: Liquid must be in the pan before heating, and the pears go in once it is at a gentle heat. They come out last.

items.label: Pour spiced syrup into the pan
Warm it gently, below a boil
Lower the pears in until fully submerged
Lift the pears out to plate

questions.prompt: Which jar on a prep shelf is truly emulsified?
questions.context: An emulsion has droplets of one liquid dispersed in another liquid. Emulsifiers can help stop the droplets from merging.
questions.explanation: Only the cloudy dressing has oil as small droplets spread through the other liquid. Dissolved sugar is a solution, and a separate oil layer is not dispersed.

options.label: A cloudy vinaigrette with tiny oil droplets spread through vinegar
A stock with a clear oil layer floating on top
A jar of plain olive oil

questions.prompt: A cook gently scoops and turns whipped egg whites into batter to keep it airy. Which menu verb fits?
questions.context: Folded = gently turned in with a scooping motion so a light mixture keeps its air.
questions.explanation: Folding is the gentle scoop-and-turn motion described on the card. The other words describe heat methods or coatings, not mixing.

questions.prompt: Link each menu word to every feature the card gives it.
questions.context: Card: Seared = browned fast on a very hot surface. Braised = browned, then slowly cooked in a little liquid. Poached = fully submerged in liquid below a boil. Roasted = dry oven air all around.
questions.explanation: Braised and poached both use liquid. Seared and braised both start with browning. Only poached is fully submerged and only roasted uses dry oven air.

questions.prompt: A dessert menu at the invented Lantern Bay Bistro lists glazed plums. What does the word promise?
questions.context: Card: Glazed = coated with a shiny layer such as syrup or sauce.
questions.explanation: Glazed describes a shiny coating on the surface. It says nothing about submerging, dispersed droplets or the method of cooking the fruit.

options.label: The plums have a shiny syrup coating
The plums were fully submerged below a boil
The plums contain dispersed oil droplets
The plums were only cooked by oven air

questions.prompt: A vegetable-focused menu offers braised fennel. Which description applies?
questions.context: Card: Braised = browned first, then cooked slowly in a little liquid in a covered pot.
questions.explanation: Braising means browning, then slow covered cooking in a small amount of liquid. The ingredient being fennel does not change what the method word means.

options.label: Browned, then slowly cooked covered in a little liquid
Quickly browned on a very hot surface and served
Fully submerged in liquid kept below a boil
Folded gently into a light batter

title: Mise en Place Race
description: Arrange prep steps for four simple recipes using the move arrows, then fix four mixed-up step lists by choosing the single move that repairs each one.

sections.title: Order the Recipe
sections.description: Use the move arrows to put steps in any order that follows the rules.

sections.title: Fix the Mix-Up
sections.description: Pick the move that repairs the list.

questions.prompt: Put these pancake steps in a workable order.
questions.context: Rules: the pan heats while you prepare, batter must be whisked before it is poured, and the pan must be hot before pouring. Pouring comes before flipping.
questions.explanation: Heating the pan is independent of measuring and whisking, so it can go early or mid-way, but it must come before pouring. One valid order: heat, measure, whisk, pour, flip.

questions.prompt: Order this vegetable stir-fry so nothing is added before it is ready.
questions.context: Rules: vegetables must be chopped and the oil hot before they go in. Sauce goes in after stir-frying begins, and plating is last.
questions.explanation: Chopping and heating oil can happen in either order, but both must precede stir-frying. Sauce then follows, and serving closes the recipe. One valid order: chop, heat, stir-fry, sauce, serve.

questions.prompt: Sequence this grilled cheese sandwich using the buttering rule.
questions.context: Rules: cheese is sliced before it goes between the bread. Butter goes on the outside of the bread, either before or after assembling, but before the sandwich is toasted. Cutting is last.

items.label: Butter the outside of the bread
Toast the sandwich in a pan

questions.explanation: Buttering only needs to happen before toasting, so it may come before or after assembly. Slicing must precede assembly. One valid order: slice, butter, assemble, toast, cut.

questions.prompt: Order this fruit salad, which has two separate prep tracks that meet at the end.
questions.context: Rules: fruit is washed, then cut. The lime is juiced, then the juice is whisked into dressing. Tossing needs both cut fruit and finished dressing.
questions.explanation: The fruit track (wash, cut) and the dressing track (juice, whisk) are independent, so they can interleave. Only tossing must come last. One valid order: wash, cut, juice, whisk, toss.

questions.prompt: Which single move repairs this muffin step list?
questions.context: Invented list: 1 Preheat the oven. 2 Mix the batter. 3 Pour batter into the tin. 4 Grease the tin. 5 Bake. Rule: a tin is greased before batter goes in.

options.label: Move "Grease the tin" to before "Pour batter into the tin"
Move "Mix the batter" to after "Pour batter"

questions.explanation: Only the greasing step is out of place. Fixed list: preheat, mix, grease, pour, bake. The other moves would create new problems.

questions.prompt: This soup list has one misplaced step. Which move fixes it?
questions.context: Invented list: 1 Chop the onion. 2 Add broth. 3 Soften the onion in the pot. 4 Simmer. 5 Season. Rule: onion is softened before broth goes in; seasoning is last.

options.label: Move "Add broth" to after "Soften the onion"
Move "Chop the onion" to the end

questions.explanation: Broth was added too early. Fixed list: chop, soften, add broth, simmer, season. Moving anything else leaves broth before the softened onion.

questions.prompt: A smoothie list starts with the wrong step. Which move repairs the flow?
questions.context: Invented list: 1 Blend until smooth. 2 Add banana and yogurt to the blender. 3 Put the lid on. 4 Pour into a glass. Rule: blend only with ingredients in and the lid on.

options.label: Move "Blend until smooth" to after "Put the lid on"
Move "Pour into a glass" to the start
Move "Put the lid on" to the end
Move "Add banana and yogurt" to the end

questions.explanation: Blending needs ingredients and a lid first. Fixed list: add, lid, blend, pour. Each other option leaves blending or pouring before the setup is complete.

questions.prompt: Which move fixes this cinnamon toast list?
questions.context: Invented list: 1 Spread butter on the bread. 2 Toast the bread. 3 Sprinkle cinnamon sugar. 4 Serve. Rule: bread is toasted first, then buttered, then sprinkled so the topping sticks to the butter.

options.label: Move "Toast the bread" to the start
Move "Sprinkle cinnamon sugar" to the start

questions.explanation: Toasting belongs first. Fixed list: toast, butter, sprinkle, serve. The other moves still put a step before something it depends on.

title: Receipt Riddles
description: Solve eight grocery-receipt puzzles: match invented shoppers to baskets, spot the entry that breaks a clue, and sort shoppers by item count.

sections.title: Receipt Grids
sections.description: Use every clue to assign each basket.

sections.title: Contradiction Checks
sections.description: Find the entry that breaks a rule.

sections.title: Case Closed

questions.prompt: Match each shopper to their basket using all three clues.
questions.context: Basket A: chips, popcorn (2 items). Basket B: apples, rice, beans, milk (4 items). Basket C: bread, eggs, tofu (3 items). Clues: Maya bought no fruit. Dev's basket has more items than Maya's. Lena's basket has fewer items than Maya's.
questions.explanation: Lena has fewer than Maya, who has fewer than Dev, so the counts 2, 3, 4 give Lena A, Maya C, Dev B. Basket C has no fruit, matching Maya's clue.

questions.prompt: Four shoppers, four baskets. Assign each shopper using the clues.
questions.context: A: milk, yogurt, cheese (3). B: apples, bananas (2). C: chips, cookies, nuts, soda (4). D: rice, beans, onions, tomatoes, oil (5). Snack items here: chips, cookies, nuts. Clues: Kenji's basket has the most items. Noor's basket has no dairy and no snack items. Amara has exactly one more item than Sofia.
questions.explanation: Kenji must hold D (5 items). Noor avoids dairy A and snack-filled C, so she holds B. Amara one above Sofia leaves Sofia A (3) and Amara C (4).

questions.prompt: This time, work backward: who owns each basket?
questions.context: A: eggs, bread (2 items). B: pasta, sauce, basil, cheese, lemons (5). C: crackers, popcorn, pretzels (3). D: oranges, rice, tea, beans (4). Snack items: crackers, popcorn, pretzels. Clues: Tomás bought only snacks. Zanele bought cheese. Priya's basket has more items than Hana's.
questions.explanation: Snack-only is C, so Tomás holds C. Cheese is only in B, so Zanele holds B. Priya must out-count Hana among A (2) and D (4): Priya D, Hana A.

questions.prompt: Which receipt entry breaks the clue about Rosa's basket?
questions.context: Clue: Rosa's basket has exactly 4 items, none of them snacks. Snack items here: chips, cookies, popcorn. Rosa's receipt lists one unit each of the entries below.
questions.explanation: The count of four is fine, but chips are a snack. That single entry contradicts the clue, while rice, beans and milk all comply.

questions.prompt: Which shopper's receipt breaks the clue that every basket has exactly 3 units?
questions.context: Count every unit. Mina: rice x2, tea x1. Pablo: eggs x2, bread x1. Yuki: soup x1, apples x2, salt x1. Dara: oats x1, milk x1, nuts x1.
questions.explanation: Mina, Pablo and Dara each total 3 units. Yuki's receipt adds 1 + 2 + 1 = 4 units, so it is the one that breaks the clue.

questions.prompt: Match each basket to its total number of units.
questions.context: P: tea x1, rice x2. Q: eggs x2, bread x1, jam x1. R: beans x1, corn x1, salsa x1. S: milk x2, oats x1, pears x1, honey x1.
questions.explanation: P and R both total 3 units, Q totals 2 + 1 + 1 = 4, and S totals 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 5. Several baskets can share one count.

questions.prompt: Who holds basket C?
questions.context: A: rice x3, tea x1 (4 units). B: chips x2, nuts x1 (3 units, all snacks). C: apples x1, milk x1 (2 units). Clues: Maya bought no fruit. Dev's basket has more units than Maya's. Sana did not buy the snack-only basket.
questions.explanation: Maya avoids fruit, so she holds A or B. Dev must out-count her, which rules out A for Maya. So Maya has B, Dev has A, and Sana has C.

questions.prompt: Order the shoppers from fewest items to most items.
questions.context: Ana has 2 more items than Bo. Bo has 1 more item than Cai. Dee has fewer items than Cai.
questions.explanation: Cai is one below Bo, Ana is two above Bo, and Dee is below Cai. That chain gives Dee, Cai, Bo, Ana with no other valid order.

title: Dinner on a Deadline
description: Solve eight scheduling puzzles about a made-up dinner: order prep tasks, assign dishes to burners, work out start times and idle gaps, and plan the final serving.

questions.prompt: Put the salad prep tasks in an order that respects every rule.
questions.context: Rules: lettuce must be washed before it is dried, and dried before it is torn into the bowl. Tossing needs both the torn lettuce and the whisked dressing. Whisking can happen any time before tossing.
questions.explanation: Washing, drying and tearing form one chain, and tossing comes after both that chain and the dressing. The whisking step can slot in anywhere before the toss.

questions.prompt: Dinner is at 6:00. Which start times make all three dishes finish exactly at 6:00?
questions.context: Invented timings, one free burner per dish, no prep time: rice takes 20 minutes, sauce takes 10 minutes, salad takes 5 minutes.
questions.explanation: Count back from 6:00: 20 minutes gives 5:40, 10 minutes gives 5:50, and 5 minutes gives 5:55. The other sets finish early or late for at least one dish.

questions.prompt: All four dishes start together. Choose where each one must cook.
questions.context: Kitchen has one oven, a large burner and a small burner. Tray bake needs the oven. The soup's stockpot only fits the large burner. The noodle pot only fits the small burner. Garlic bread shares the oven rack with the tray bake.
questions.explanation: Each dish has one place that satisfies its stated constraint. The bread rides along in the oven because the rule lets it share the rack with the tray bake.

questions.prompt: With a single burner, choose each dish's start time so the last one ends at 6:00.
questions.context: Invented timings, run back to back with no gaps: sauce 10 minutes, beans 15 minutes, rice 20 minutes. Sauce goes first and rice goes last so it is hottest at 6:00.
questions.explanation: Rice must run 5:40 to 6:00. Beans fill the 15 minutes before it, from 5:25. Sauce fills the 10 minutes before that, from 5:15.

questions.prompt: Everything starts at 5:30 and dinner is 6:00. How many total minutes do finished dishes wait?
questions.context: Invented timings, a burner per dish: rice 20 minutes, sauce 10 minutes, salad 5 minutes. Count each dish's wait from when it finishes until 6:00.
questions.explanation: Rice finishes at 5:50 and waits 10, sauce finishes at 5:40 and waits 20, and salad finishes at 5:35 and waits 25. That totals 55 idle minutes.

questions.prompt: Order the plating tasks so every rule is followed.
questions.context: Rules: plates are warmed before rice goes on, and sauce goes over the rice afterward. Salad bowls can be filled any time. Everything is carried to the table last.
questions.explanation: Plates, rice and sauce form a fixed chain. The salad bowls are independent, so they can be filled anywhere before the final carry.

questions.prompt: Connect each dish to every serving tool that works for it.
questions.context: Soup is liquid. Rice is loose grains. Salad is leaves. Roasted vegetables are whole chunky pieces. The ladle moves only liquid. Tongs grip leaves or whole pieces. The serving spoon scoops loose grains or chunky pieces.
questions.explanation: Soup only suits the ladle, rice only suits the spoon, and salad only suits tongs. Roasted vegetables are whole chunky pieces, so both tongs and the spoon work.

questions.prompt: What is the latest start time for the rice so dinner lands on the table at 6:00?
questions.context: Invented timings: rice cooks 20 minutes, plating takes 4 minutes after the rice is done, and carrying to the table takes 1 minute.
questions.explanation: Carrying ends at 6:00, so it starts at 5:59. Plating starts at 5:55, meaning the rice must be done by then, so it must start by 5:35.

title: Sauce Family Tree
description: Sort recipe cards into sauce families, then trace four variations back to the base they grow from.

sections.title: Sort the families
sections.description: Use the recipe cards to place each sauce.

questions.prompt: Match each sauce card to the family its method belongs to. Several sauces can share a family.
questions.context: House framework for this quiz: Emulsion = fat or oil spread as tiny droplets in a water-based liquid. Roux = flour cooked in fat, then liquid added. Puree = blended solids give body. Reduction = liquid simmered down.

left.label: Garlic aioli-style: oil whisked slowly into egg yolk and lemon juice
Mustard vinaigrette: oil shaken hard with vinegar and a spoon of mustard
Mushroom gravy: flour cooked in butter, then stock whisked in
Cheese sauce: flour and butter cooked, milk added, cheese melted in
Roasted tomato sauce: roasted tomatoes blended smooth, no flour
Balsamic glaze: vinegar simmered until syrupy

questions.explanation: Families follow method, not cuisine: two sauces disperse oil in a watery liquid, two thicken with cooked flour and fat, one uses blended solids, one simply concentrates by simmering.

questions.prompt: These invented sauces come from different kitchens. Match each to its family using only the method described.
questions.context: All four sauces are invented for this quiz. Use the same family definitions as the previous task.

left.label: Tamarind Night Drizzle: tamarind liquid and sugar simmered to half its volume
Sesame-Lime Dressing: oil and lime juice whisked with tahini so they stay blended
Red Pepper Swirl: charred peppers and almonds blended thick, no flour
Coconut Pan Gravy: flour toasted in oil, coconut milk whisked in

questions.explanation: The same logic crosses cuisines. Tahini helps keep oil droplets from merging, toasted flour thickens the gravy, blended peppers supply body, and simmering concentrates the tamarind.

questions.prompt: A plain oil-and-vinegar dressing sits on the counter and slowly separates into layers. What best explains this?

options.label: Oil droplets merge back together because nothing keeps them apart
The vinegar cooks the oil into a roux
The oil turns into a puree of vinegar solids
The dressing reduces until the water disappears

questions.explanation: An emulsion holds droplets of one liquid in another. Without an emulsifier to inhibit droplets merging, they coalesce and the layers reappear.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of a basic roux-based milk sauce in a workable order.
questions.context: Invented step cards. Each step needs the previous one: fat must be melted before flour is stirred in, the flour is cooked before liquid goes in, and the sauce is simmered last.

items.label: Melt the butter in a pan
Simmer gently until the sauce thickens
Stir in flour and cook briefly

questions.explanation: A roux starts with fat and flour cooked together; adding liquid gradually comes next, and the final simmer finishes the thickening.

questions.prompt: Smoky Chipotle Spread blends smoked chilli paste into a thick whisked sauce of egg yolk and oil. Which base does it grow from?
questions.explanation: The chilli paste is a flavour add-on. The thick body comes from oil dispersed in egg yolk, so this is an emulsion variation.

questions.prompt: Golden Onion Velouté thickens stock with cooked flour and butter, then adds softened onion flavour. Which base is it?
questions.explanation: Flour cooked in fat and then loosened with liquid is the roux method, so the onion version is a branch of that family.

questions.prompt: After searing, a cook boils wine and stock until half remains and the sauce turns glossy. Which base is this pan sauce?
questions.explanation: No flour, oil droplets or blended solids are involved. Boiling away liquid concentrates flavour and body, which defines a reduction.

questions.prompt: Spicy Carrot-Ginger Sauce simmers carrots until soft, then blends them smooth with no flour. Which base does it grow from?
questions.explanation: Its thickness comes from finely blended carrot solids, the puree approach, rather than from cooked flour or dispersed droplets.

title: Cookware Casting Call
description: Cast the right pan, pot or dish for eight kitchen jobs by matching stated properties to tasks, ordering a bench log and checking when several tools qualify.

questions.prompt: Which card should be cast for searing several cold items in a row with the smallest temperature drop?
questions.context: Invented spec cards. A: cast iron skillet, heat retention high, slow to heat. B: thin aluminum skillet, retention low, heats fast. C: glass baking dish, oven only. D: stainless-clad skillet, retention medium.
questions.explanation: High retention means the metal holds stored heat when cold food lands on it. Medium or low retention drops more, and the glass dish cannot go on a burner.

questions.prompt: Match each kitchen job to the cookware type whose stated properties fit it.
questions.context: Invented cards. Thin saucepan: light, 2 L, heats and cools fast. Dutch oven: heavy, tight lid, holds steady heat. Stainless stockpot: 8 L, light for its size, fast to boil.

left.label: Reheat one cup of soup, adjusting heat often
Hold steady low heat through a long braise
Boil water for a 6 L batch
Simmer 1 L of sauce, then cool the pot quickly

questions.explanation: Small, quick-response jobs suit the thin saucepan, steady long heat suits the heavy lidded pot, and only the stockpot has the 6 L capacity.

questions.prompt: A baked pasta must be checked for browning at the bottom edges without lifting it. Which vessel meets that requirement?
questions.context: Invented cards. All four are oven-safe for this task.

options.label: Glass baking dish with clear sides
Cast iron skillet with opaque sides
Aluminum sheet pan with opaque base
Enameled Dutch oven with opaque walls

questions.explanation: Only the glass dish lets you see the sides and base while it bakes. The other vessels are opaque, so checking means lifting or opening them.

questions.prompt: For each need, choose the material trait that explains it.
questions.context: Thermal mass means how much heat a pan stores per degree. High thermal mass warms slowly, cools slowly and usually weighs more. Low thermal mass does the opposite.

cells.label: Stays hot after cold food is added
Reacts quickly when the burner is turned down
Takes longer to preheat on the same burner

questions.explanation: Storing more heat is the same property that resists temperature drops, delays warming and slows reaction to burner changes.

questions.prompt: A recipe sears on the stovetop, then finishes in a 220°C oven in the same pan. Which card qualifies?
questions.context: Invented spec cards, all 28 cm. Nonstick skillet: stovetop yes, oven limit 180°C. Stainless-clad skillet: stovetop yes, oven limit 260°C. Glass dish: stovetop no, oven limit 230°C. Thin saucepan: stovetop yes, oven no.
questions.explanation: The task needs both stovetop use and an oven limit of at least 220°C. Only the stainless-clad card meets both stated requirements.

questions.prompt: Using the bench log, order the pans from quickest to slowest to reach the target surface temperature.
questions.context: Invented bench log, same burner and setting. Cast iron skillet: 6 minutes. Thin aluminum skillet: 2 minutes. Enameled Dutch oven: 9 minutes. Stainless-clad skillet: 4 minutes.
questions.explanation: Sorting the logged times gives 2, 4, 6 and 9 minutes: aluminum, stainless-clad, cast iron, then the Dutch oven.

questions.prompt: Connect every job to every tool that meets all of its stated requirements.
questions.context: Invented tools. Saucepan: stovetop, lid, no oven, 2 L. Stockpot: stovetop, lid, oven, 6 L. Dutch oven: stovetop, lid, oven, 5 L. Glass dish: oven only, no lid, 3 L. Job 1: simmer 1.5 L on the stovetop with a lid. Job 2: start on the stove, finish in the oven, with a lid, 5 L batch. Job 3: oven-only bake of 2.5 L, no lid needed.

left.label: Job 2: stove to oven, lid, 5 L

questions.explanation: Job 1 fits three tools, Job 2 fits the two oven-safe lidded tools with enough capacity, and Job 3 fits the stockpot, Dutch oven and glass dish. The saucepan fails the oven jobs.

questions.prompt: Two skillets meet every listed requirement. Which extra constraint would make the choice unique?

title: Kitchen Sound Guess
description: Play six short synthetic sound cues, match each to a kitchen action using a printed legend, then judge what a sound alone can and cannot tell you.

sections.title: Match the cue
sections.description: Six clips, one action each.

sections.title: What can sound not tell you?
sections.description: Spot claims the cue cannot establish.

questions.prompt: Play the cue. Which kitchen action does this pattern represent?
questions.context: Legend: Whisk = six quick tones alternating between a lower and a higher pitch. Chop = four slow, evenly spaced low beats. Pour = three long falling steps. Grate = a rising run of five short tones.
questions.explanation: Six fast tones alternating between two pitches match the whisk pattern. This identifies the motion only, not what is being whisked or how it turned out.
questions.transcript: Six short triangle-wave tones, 0.15 seconds apart, alternating 600 Hz and 700 Hz, starting on 600 Hz.

questions.prompt: Play the cue. Which action does this evenly spaced pattern match?
questions.context: Legend: Chop = four slow, evenly spaced low beats. Snap = one very short top-pitched tone. Blend = one continuous low hum. Sizzle = eight rapid identical high pulses.
questions.explanation: Four low beats separated by equal half-second gaps match the chop pattern. The steady spacing is the clue; the other legend entries have different counts, pitch or length.
questions.transcript: Four identical 250 Hz triangle-wave beats, each 0.15 seconds long, starting every 0.5 seconds.

questions.prompt: Play the cue. Which action does the falling pattern represent?
questions.context: Legend: Pour = three long falling steps. Whisk = six quick alternating high-low tones. Chop = four slow, evenly spaced low beats. Snap = one very short top-pitched tone.
questions.explanation: Three long tones that step downward match the pour pattern. Whisk alternates quickly, chop stays at one low pitch, and snap is a single brief tone.
questions.transcript: Three sine tones of 0.4 seconds each, stepping down from 800 Hz to 650 Hz to 500 Hz with tiny gaps between them.

questions.prompt: Play the cue. Which action does this single brief tone represent?
questions.context: Legend: Snap = one very short top-pitched tone. Blend = one continuous low hum. Chop = four slow, evenly spaced low beats. Pour = three long falling steps.
questions.explanation: One very short, high tone followed by silence matches the snap pattern. Blend would be long and low, chop would repeat four times, and pour would have three steps.
questions.transcript: A single 1000 Hz triangle-wave tone lasting 0.08 seconds, then silence.

questions.prompt: Play the cue. Which action matches this long, steady, low sound?
questions.context: Legend: Blend = one continuous low hum. Snap = one very short top-pitched tone. Whisk = six quick alternating high-low tones. Grate = a rising run of five short tones.
questions.explanation: A steady 220 Hz hum with no pitch change matches the blend pattern. Grate would rise in steps, whisk would alternate, and snap would be one brief high tone.
questions.transcript: Three joined 0.4-second sine tones at a constant 220 Hz, forming one steady low hum about 1.2 seconds long.

questions.prompt: Play the cue. Which action matches this fast run of identical pulses?
questions.context: Legend: Sizzle = eight rapid identical high pulses. Whisk = six quick alternating high-low tones. Chop = four slow, evenly spaced low beats. Pour = three long falling steps.
questions.explanation: Eight identical high pulses in quick succession match the sizzle pattern. Whisk alternates two pitches and has six tones, so it does not fit.
questions.transcript: Eight identical 900 Hz triangle-wave pulses, each 0.08 seconds long, starting every 0.1 seconds.

questions.prompt: A listener hears the Chop cue: four low beats, equally spaced. What can the sound alone not establish?
questions.context: The cue is a synthetic pattern, not a recording of a real ingredient. Only its pitch, count, spacing and length are available to the listener.
questions.explanation: Pitch, count and spacing are all in the cue. Nothing in four identical beats reveals which ingredient was being cut.

options.label: The cuts came at equal intervals
There were four beats in total
The beats were low in pitch

questions.prompt: For the Sizzle cue, decide whether the sound alone establishes each claim.
questions.context: The Sizzle cue is eight identical 900 Hz pulses, 0.1 seconds apart. It is a synthetic pattern and carries no information about temperature or readiness.
questions.explanation: Pulse count and pace are directly in the cue. Doneness and pan temperature are not encoded in it, so a listener would be guessing.

cells.label: The pulses were rapid and evenly paced
The pan had reached a specific temperature

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: The sounds are original synthetic tone patterns, not recordings of real kitchens. Each question prints a legend, and a written transcript describes every cue, so the quiz can be played without audio. The sounds never indicate doneness, temperature or safety.

diagram.title: Counter six: schematic top row and bottom strip

questions.prompt: Match each counter tool to the invented dish card that uses it.
questions.context: Card A, pancakes: whisk batter, flip with a flat tool. Card B, dressing: shake oil, lemon juice and mustard in a screw-top jar. Card C, rice: rinse in a sieve, simmer in a lidded pot.

title: Dish Rack Logic
description: Solve small fictional dish-rack puzzles by placing cups, plates and utensil caddies from size and adjacency clues, then repair broken layouts and count placements.

questions.prompt: Fill each slot of this four-slot rack so every rule holds.
questions.context: Slots 1–4 run left to right. A shelf hangs over slots 1 and 2; slots 3 and 4 are open. Items: short cup, bowl, tall cup, utensil caddy. Rules: the tall cup cannot sit under the shelf. The bowl sits immediately left of the tall cup. The caddy must be in an open slot.
questions.explanation: The tall cup must be in slot 3 or 4. If it were in 4, the bowl would be in 3 and the caddy stuck under the shelf, so the tall cup is in 3.

questions.prompt: Place the plate, which fills two adjacent slots, and the other items in this five-slot rack.
questions.context: Slots 1–5 run left to right; a shelf covers slots 4 and 5. Items: one plate (two adjacent slots), tall cup, mug, bowl. Rules: the tall cup and the plate cannot be under the shelf. The mug must touch the plate.
questions.explanation: The plate and tall cup need the three open slots, so the mug and bowl are under the shelf. Touching the plate forces the plate into slots 2–3 and the mug into 4.

questions.prompt: Fill this two-row, two-column rack so all three rules are satisfied.
questions.context: Positions: top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right. Items: tall cup, wide bowl, mug, utensil caddy. Rules: the tall cup and wide bowl both need the roomy bottom row. The mug sits directly above the wide bowl. The tall cup is in the right column.
questions.explanation: The bottom row holds the tall cup and bowl, so the mug and caddy are on top. The tall cup takes bottom-right, the bowl bottom-left, and the mug goes above the bowl.

questions.prompt: Which single swap leaves this layout with no broken rule?
questions.context: Current slots 1–5: Mug, Plate, Plate, Tall cup, Bowl. A shelf covers slots 4 and 5. Rules: tall cups and plates cannot be under the shelf; each plate fills two adjacent slots; the bowl must not touch the tall cup.

options.label: Swap the tall cup with the bowl
Swap the tall cup with the mug
Swap the tall cup with the right plate slot
Swap the mug with the bowl

questions.explanation: Only moving the tall cup to slot 1 clears the shelf without splitting the plate, and the bowl then stays away from it. The other swaps leave the cup under the shelf or break the plate.

questions.prompt: Which single swap removes every conflict in this six-slot rack?
questions.context: Current slots 1–6: Cup, Caddy, Plate, Plate, Bowl, Cup. Rules: the caddy must be in an end slot (1 or 6); no cup may touch the caddy; each plate fills two adjacent slots.

options.label: Swap the caddy with the slot 1 cup
Swap the caddy with the bowl
Swap the caddy with the slot 6 cup
Swap the caddy with the left plate slot

questions.explanation: Moving the caddy to slot 6 puts it at an end beside the bowl, away from cups. Swapping with slot 1 leaves a cup touching it, and the other swaps fail.

questions.prompt: How many different ways can the two plates be placed in this rack?
questions.context: A rack has six slots in a row, 1–6, with no shelf. Each plate fills two adjacent slots. The two plates are identical and cannot overlap. Empty slots are allowed.
questions.explanation: Treat each plate as one block, leaving two single slots; choose which two of the four positions hold plates: 6 ways, such as 1–2 with 3–4 or 2–3 with 5–6.

questions.prompt: Arrange the loading steps in any order that follows the rack's clearance rules.

title: Seven Guests, Four Servings
description: Scale a four-serving pancake recipe up to seven guests and three more invented recipe tables with explicit serving ratios, then inspect four more tables to find the ingredient row that was scaled wrongly.

sections.title: Fill the tables
sections.description: Work out the missing quantities from the serving ratio.

sections.title: Catch the slip
sections.description: Each table has exactly one row that breaks the ratio.

questions.prompt: Seven guests are coming and each gets one serving. Scale this pancake batter from 4 servings to 7 servings. Choose the correct value for every cell.
questions.context: Invented recipe for 4 servings: flour 300 g, milk 240 ml, butter 60 g. Scale every ingredient by the same serving ratio, 7 divided by 4. Quantities are metric and exact; no rounding is needed.
questions.explanation: Seven servings divided by four servings gives 1.75. Every ingredient is multiplied by 1.75, so flour becomes 525 g, milk 420 ml and butter 105 g.

questions.prompt: An invented lentil soup serves 5. Scale it for 7 guests by using one ratio for all rows.
questions.context: Invented recipe for 5 servings: lentils 200 g, stock 1000 ml, carrots 150 g. The ratio is 7 divided by 5. Declared metric units only; results are whole numbers.
questions.explanation: The ratio is 1.4. Multiplying gives 200 × 1.4 = 280 g lentils, 1000 × 1.4 = 1400 ml stock and 150 × 1.4 = 210 g carrots.

questions.prompt: Scale this invented rice pudding down from 8 servings to 3. Fill each cell using the same ratio.
questions.context: Invented recipe for 8 servings: rice 160 g, milk 1200 ml, sugar 72 g. Use ratio 3 divided by 8. Use the stated metric units; every result here is a whole number, so no rounding is needed.
questions.explanation: The ratio is 0.375. So 160 g becomes 60 g, 1200 ml becomes 450 ml, and 72 g becomes 27 g.

questions.prompt: An invented tomato sauce makes 6 servings. Work out the ratio and quantities needed for 4 servings.
questions.context: Invented recipe for 6 servings: tomatoes 900 g, oil 30 ml, salt 12 g. Scale all three rows by the same fraction. Use declared metric units; the results are whole numbers.
questions.explanation: Four servings over six servings is 2/3. That gives 900 × 2/3 = 600 g, 30 × 2/3 = 20 ml and 12 × 2/3 = 8 g.

questions.prompt: This porridge was scaled from 4 to 10 servings, a multiplier of 2.5. Which row breaks that multiplier?
questions.context: Invented table, original → scaled: oats 120 g → 300 g; milk 400 ml → 1000 ml; honey 20 g → 40 g; seeds 16 g → 40 g.
questions.explanation: Honey should be 20 × 2.5 = 50 g, not 40 g. The oats, milk and seeds rows all match the 2.5 multiplier.

questions.prompt: A cake card was scaled from 6 to 9 servings, a multiplier of 1.5. Which scaled row is wrong?
questions.context: Invented table, original → scaled: flour 400 g → 600 g; butter 90 g → 145 g; sugar 150 g → 225 g; cocoa 30 g → 45 g.
questions.explanation: Butter should be 90 × 1.5 = 135 g. The other three rows each equal their original quantity times 1.5.

questions.prompt: A rice dish was reduced from 8 servings to 2, so every row should be one quarter. Find the faulty row.
questions.context: Invented table, original → scaled: rice 320 g → 80 g; stock 1200 ml → 300 ml; oil 60 ml → 15 ml; peas 200 g → 100 g.
questions.explanation: Peas should be 200 ÷ 4 = 50 g. The 100 g shown is half the original, so it used the wrong factor.

questions.prompt: A hummus card was scaled from 3 to 5 servings, a multiplier of 5/3. Which row does not follow it?
questions.context: Invented table, original → scaled: yogurt 120 g → 180 g; chickpeas 180 g → 300 g; tahini 45 g → 75 g; lemon juice 30 ml → 50 ml.
questions.explanation: Yogurt should be 120 × 5/3 = 200 g, not 180 g. Chickpeas, tahini and lemon juice all work out exactly.

questions.prompt: Guests arrive soon for a big viewing night. How do you lay out the snack table?

A tiered display with one eye-catching focal platter

Put the effort into one impressive item and keep the rest simple
Work down a written checklist so nothing is forgotten
Set out a few basics and see what the room needs

questions.explanation: Both approaches work. Plain choices serve steady grazing, themed lineups serve showpiece hosting, and asking guests keeps the table adaptable.

Ask guests what they like as they arrive and top up from there
Stage a playful taste challenge around the spiciest items

Bring out a backup tray prepared earlier in one big refresh
Grab whatever is in the kitchen and refill gaps as I notice them
Recruit guests to help and turn the restock into a mini event

questions.prompt: A guest walks in with a surprise dish nobody expected. Where does it go?

In a space I already reserved for guest contributions
Rearrange the table so it becomes the new centerpiece
Add it to my themed display with a small label card

questions.prompt: Plates and napkins run low during the loudest stretch of the night. How do you respond?
questions.explanation: Supplies are part of the table too. A stash is plan-ahead grazing, a dramatic restock is ad-lib showmanship, and the other answers sit between.

options.label: Pull a stack of extras I stashed nearby
Make a quick, lively restock run when the action dips
Use whatever is on hand, like paper towels or small bowls
Reset the whole table at the next break around a featured dish

questions.prompt: Rank these hosting priorities from most important (top) to least important (bottom).

Everything is ready before guests arrive
Room to add or swap dishes on the fly
